I think you're comparing two different situations here, and it does not really hold up once you look at what I actually said. Asking someone to point to explicit text when nothing has been offered is one thing. That is not what happened here. I did not just demand a citation from Piers while offering nothing myself. I gave an actual case, Sherrill versus Knight, along with a more recent appellate ruling in the AP versus Trump case, both of which are real, named legal decisions with an actual holding behind them. That is a very different position from someone just saying prove it with no basis of their own.

In case you did not get a chance to read it, here is what I actually laid out in that link.

I said that there is a real legal difference depending on which part of the White House we are talking about, and that courts have already ruled on it. For the larger, generally open spaces, the press briefing room, the East Room, White House grounds broadly, once the government opens those spaces to press as a standard practice, courts have said it cannot then turn around and exclude specific outlets based on their viewpoint. That principle goes back to a 1977 case called Sherrill versus Knight, and it got reaffirmed last year when a federal judge, appointed by Trump himself, ruled that once the government opens its doors to some journalists, whether that is the Oval Office, the East Room, or anywhere else, it cannot slam those doors shut on others just because of their viewpoint.

But I also said that ruling did not survive appeal in full. A federal appeals court later overturned most of it, and specifically named the Oval Office, Air Force One, and Mar a Lago, his residence, as spaces that are not First Amendment public forums opened for general discussion. The court stated outright that the White House retains discretion to determine, including on the basis of viewpoint, which journalists get admitted to those specific spaces. The one thing the appeals court preserved was the East Room, since that is a space where all pre credentialed media is typically invited as standard practice, so viewpoint neutral access still applies there.

So my actual point was never that Trump is fully justified no matter what. I said it depends entirely on which space we are talking about. If this ban applies to the general press spaces, the briefing room, the East Room, broadly open events, that runs into the same legal wall the AP case already established. But if it is specifically about access to his office or his residence, courts have already said he has real discretion there, including the ability to exclude specific outlets based on viewpoint.

Comparing that to asking for the legal text on abortion does not really work, because that comparison only makes sense against someone demanding a citation while giving nothing themselves. I did the opposite. I gave the citation and laid out exactly how the courts have drawn the line. If you disagree with my read of those cases, I am genuinely open to hearing why. But this was not a gotcha question with nothing behind it. It was a sourced legal argument, and I would rather you engage with the actual cases than compare it to a completely separate legal debate that does not really apply here.

Capricorn bioceanic corridor, connecting the Brazilian port of Santos with the Chilean ports of Antofagasta and Tarapaca, and traversing Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina and Chile, has sparked tremendous enthusiasm throughout the region. Formally launched in 2022, discussions about building it actually date back to 1960-70. It was completed in June of this year when the beautiful Bioceanic Bridge between Brazil and Paraguay over the Paraguay River was finished. Consisting of highways, bridges, border crossings, etc. Capricorn doesn’t represent the level of sophistication of the proposed Chinese-Brazilian high-speed rail corridor between Brazil’s port of Santos and Peru’s Chancay megaport. But there is a great sense of accomplishment and excitement that Capricorn is completed and offers new opportunities for the entire South American region.

OFFICIAL NAME:
Holy See

Note: The Holy See is the universal government of the Catholic Church and operates from the Vatican City State, a sovereign, independent territory of 0.44 square kilometers (0.17 square miles). The Pope is the ruler of both the Vatican City State and the Holy See. The Holy See, as the supreme body of government of the Catholic Church, is a sovereign juridical entity under international law.

Geography and People
Area: Total of 0.44 sq. km. (109 acres).
Population (July 2008 est.): 824 (citizens and non-citizens). Citizens: 546 (467 of which are resident).
Ethnic groups: Italian, Swiss, other.
Religion: Roman Catholic.
Languages: Italian, Latin, French, various others.
Literacy: 100%.
Work force: 3,000 lay workers (reside outside the Vatican).

Government
Type: Papacy; ecclesiastical, governmental, and administrative capital of the Roman Catholic Church.
Independence: Sovereign entity since medieval times (Lateran Pacts creating the Vatican City State and confirming independence and sovereignty of the Holy See signed with Italy on February 11, 1929).
Suffrage: Limited to Cardinals less than 80 years old.

Economy
Budget: Revenues (2007) $372 million; expenditures (2007) $386 million.
Industries: Worldwide banking and financial activities; printing; production of coins, medals, postage stamps, a small amount of mosaics, and staff uniforms. This unique, noncommercial economy is also supported financially by contributions (known as Peter's Pence) from Roman Catholics throughout the world, the sale of postage stamps and tourist mementos, fees from admissions to museums, and the sale of publications. The incomes and living standards of lay workers are comparable to, or somewhat better than, those of counterparts who work in the city of Rome.

PEOPLE AND HISTORY
Almost all of Vatican City's citizens live inside the Vatican's walls. The Vatican includes high-ranking dignitaries, priests, nuns, and guards as well as about 3,000 lay workers who comprise the majority of the work force.

The Holy See's diplomatic history began in the fourth century, but the boundaries of the papacy's temporal power have shifted over the centuries. From the 8th century through the middle of the 19th century, the Popes held sway over the Papal States, which included a broad band of territory across central Italy. In 1860, after prolonged civil and regional unrest, Victor Emmanuel's army seized the Papal States, leaving only Rome and surrounding coastal regions under papal control.

In 1870, Victor Emmanuel captured Rome itself and declared it the new capital of Italy, ending papal claims to temporal power. Pope Pius IX and his successors disputed the legitimacy of these acts and proclaimed themselves to be "prisoners" in the Vatican. Finally, in 1929, the Italian Government and the Holy See signed three agreements resolving the dispute:

A treaty recognizing the independence and sovereignty of the Holy See and creating the State of the Vatican City;
A concordat defining the relations between the government and the church within Italy; and
A financial convention providing the Holy See with compensation for its losses in 1870.
A revised concordat, altering the terms of church-state relations, was signed in 1984.

Principal Government Officials

Holy See:
Head of State--Pope Benedict XVI
Secretary of State (Prime Minister)--Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone
Deputy Secretary of State--Archbishop Fernando Filoni
Secretary for Relations with States (Foreign Minister)--Archbishop Dominique Mamberti
Apostolic Nuncio (equivalent to Ambassador) to the United States--Archbishop Pietro Sambi

The Holy See maintains an Apostolic Nunciature, the equivalent of an embassy, in the U.S. at 3339 Massachusetts Ave. NW, Washington, DC 20008, (202) 333-7121.

Vatican City State:
Head of State--Pope Benedict XVI
President of the Vatican City State Governorate--Cardinal Giovanni Lajolo

Papal Audiences
The North American College in Rome, owned and operated by the U.S. Catholic hierarchy for training American priests, handles requests for papal audiences. The address is Casa Santa Maria dell'Umilta, Via dell'Umilta 30, 00187, Rome, Italy (tel. 39-06-690-0189).

U.S.-HOLY SEE RELATIONS
The United States maintained consular relations with the Papal States from 1797 to 1870 and diplomatic relations with the Pope, in his capacity as head of the Papal States, from 1848 to 1868, though not at the ambassadorial level. These relations lapsed with the loss of all papal territories in 1870.

From 1870 to 1984, the United States did not have diplomatic relations with the Holy See. Several presidents, however, designated personal envoys to visit the Holy See periodically for discussions of international humanitarian and political issues. Myron C. Taylor was the first of these representatives, serving from 1939 to 1950. Presidents Nixon, Ford, Carter, and Reagan also appointed personal envoys to the Pope.

The United States and the Holy See announced the establishment of diplomatic relations on January 10, 1984. On March 7, 1984, the Senate confirmed William A. Wilson as the first U.S. ambassador to the Holy See. Ambassador Wilson had been President Reagan's personal envoy to the Pope since 1981. The Holy See named Archbishop Pio Laghi as the first Apostolic Nuncio (equivalent to ambassador) of the Holy See to the U.S.

The U.S.-Holy See relationship is best characterized as an active global partnership for human dignity. Establishment of diplomatic relations has bolstered the frequent contact and consultation between the United States and the Holy See on many important international issues of mutual interest. The commitment to human dignity at the core of both the U.S. and Holy See approach to the world gives rise to a common agenda for action to promote religious freedom, justice, religious and ethnic tolerance, liberty, respect for women and children and for the rule of law.

Holy See priorities for 2008 include freedom of religion, inter-religious dialogue (particularly with the Muslim world), ecumenism, protection for the traditional family, and peace (particularly for the Middle East). Pope Benedict XVI has also publicly expressed concern over the issue of climate change, describing the protection of the environment as a moral responsibility to safeguard God's creation.

Principal U.S. Embassy Official
Ambassador--Mary Ann Glendon

The U.S. Embassy to the Holy See is located in Rome in the Villa Domiziana, Via delle Terme Deciane 26, 00153 Rome, Italy, Tel: (396) 4674-3428.

Full Text Of Pope Francis' Remarks To Congress
September 24, 2015 | by NCC Staff
Mr. Vice-President,

Mr. Speaker,

Honorable Members of Congress, Dear Friends,

I am most grateful for your invitation to address this Joint Session of Congress in "the land of the free and the home of the brave". I would like to think that the reason for this is that I too am a son of this great continent, from which we have all received so much and toward which we share a common responsibility.

Each son or daughter of a given country has a mission, a personal and social responsibility. Your own responsibility as members of Congress is to enable this country, by your legislative activity, to grow as a nation. You are the face of its people, their representatives. You are called to defend and preserve the dignity of your fellow citizens in the tireless and demanding pursuit of the common good, for this is the chief aim of all politics. A political society endures when it seeks, as a vocation, to satisfy common needs by stimulating the growth of all its members, especially those in situations of greater vulnerability or risk. Legislative activity is always based on care for the people. To this you have been invited, called and convened by those who elected you.

Yours is a work which makes me reflect in two ways on the figure of Moses. On the one hand, the patriarch and lawgiver of the people of Israel symbolizes the need of peoples to keep alive their sense of unity by means of just legislation. On the other, the figure of Moses leads us directly to God and thus to the transcendent dignity of the human being. Moses provides us with a good synthesis of your work: you are asked to protect, by means of the law, the image and likeness fashioned by God on every human face.

Today I would like not only to address you, but through you the entire people of the United States. Here, together with their representatives, I would like to take this opportunity to dialogue with the many thousands of men and women who strive each day to do an honest day’s work, to bring home their daily bread, to save money and –one step at a time – to build a better life for their families. These are men and women who are not concerned simply with paying their taxes, but in their own quiet way sustain the life of society. They generate solidarity by their actions, and they create organizations which offer a helping hand to those most in need.

I would also like to enter into dialogue with the many elderly persons who are a storehouse of wisdom forged by experience, and who seek in many ways, especially through volunteer work, to share their stories and their insights. I know that many of them are retired, but still active; they keep working to build up this land. I also want to dialogue with all those young people who are working to realize their great and noble aspirations, who are not led astray by facile proposals, and who face difficult situations, often as a result of immaturity on the part of many adults. I wish to dialogue with all of you, and I would like to do so through the historical memory of your people.

🔧 BAY PATH — BUILDING PATHWAYS FOR OUR COMMUNITIES 🎓
At our Lions Club meeting tonight, Lion Kevin Congdon welcomed Kyle Brenner, Superintendent-Director of Bay Path Regional Vocational Technical High School, along with Kirsten Congdon, Southbridge’s representative on the Bay Path School Committee.
Kyle shared an informative look at what’s happening at Bay Path and the important role the school plays in our region.
Bay Path offers 23 different vocational programs, including its newest program, Diesel Technology. These programs are developed not only to meet state requirements, but also with input from professionals who are working in the trades today. That helps students gain the practical skills and experience they need to move directly into careers or continue their education.
And the demand is certainly there. Kyle explained that Bay Path currently receives about three applications for every available seat. The existing facility limits how many students can be accepted, leaving many young people on a waiting list who would like the opportunity to attend.
Kyle also discussed a major change affecting vocational schools across Massachusetts: a new lottery-based admissions system mandated by the state. Because the system is so new, there is not yet enough information to know what its long-term impact will be on Bay Path and students from our local communities.
Bay Path’s impact goes beyond high school students. Adult education is returning, along with CTI training opportunities designed to help people who are unemployed or underemployed develop skills that can lead to good jobs and new careers.
Bay Path serves students from 10 communities, providing young people—and now more adults—with another pathway toward a successful future.
The Southbridge Lions have a special connection to Bay Path as well. Many of our own Lions are proud Bay Path graduates! 🦁
Thank you to Kyle and Kirsten for joining us, and a special thank-you to Lion Kevin Congdon for arranging an excellent and very timely program. @BayPathSuper
